- Target TTFT (time-to-first-token): Acme ideally wants median <= 200ms and p95 <= 400ms for interactive chat flows.

- Optimizations: prefix/KV warm caching, tuned batching windows, and quantization profiles that can materially reduce TTFT.

Thanks Marissa  nice recap. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 

1) TTFT expectations: median <= 200ms is our aspiration; we can tolerate p95 up to ~400ms for most flows, but for live chat we want to avoid >500ms p95 if possible.
2) Concurrency/throughput: 200 RPS peak is accurate for the next quarter; concurrency (open streaming sessions) will hit ~50-60 concurrently in some campaigns.
3) Streaming: SSE is preferred for our web client because we avoid extra infra; however, our mobile team might request WebSocket for lower overhead in poor networks. Can Redwood support both simultaneously?
4) Chunk cadence: 100-200ms is ideal. For some low-latency prompts we may want tighter cadence (75-100ms).

Hi Samir / Priya  looping in a bit more technical detail and a proposed benchmark plan.

Short answers: yes, Redwood supports both SSE and WebSocket simultaneously. We recommend SSE for browser-first flows for simplicity; WebSocket offers lower protocol overhead and client multiplexing if you need it on mobile.

TTFT specifics (what we can deliver and tradeoffs):
- Hosted (shared capacity): typical TTFT for a 7B-class model is 250-400ms median depending on sequence length and tokenization; p95 can spike >500ms under noisy shared load.
- Dedicated: with pinned GPUs, warm KV/prefix caching, and tuned batching we routinely hit median TTFT in the 100-180ms range on 7B/ggml-quantized variants and p95 under 350-400ms for representative workloads.
- Private (on-prem/VPC): similar to Dedicated but depends on your HW profile; we'll provide guidance for CPU/GPU specs.

Streaming & chunk cadence:
- Redwood streams tokens as soon as they are available; chunk cadence is configurable via our streaming buffer window. For the cadence you requested (100-200ms) we can configure small buffer windows while keeping throughput efficient. Tightening to ~75-100ms is possible but increases compute overhead per token (more calls, smaller batches).
- First-chunk latency: with warm caches and precompiled kernels we can get the first byte out typically in 60-140ms on Dedicated for short prompts. Factors: model size, request context length, and whether KV cache can be reused.

Concurrency & throughput guidance:
- For 200 RPS and ~50 concurrent streams, Dedicated nodes sized for inference (N GPUs, model-dependent) with autoscaling and burst capacity will meet the SLOs; we'll map instance profiles during the benchmark.

Proposed benchmark plan:
1) You share the sample prompt set + model variant (acme/open-dialog-v2) and representative payload sizes.
2) We run a controlled benchmark over Dedicated trial capacity with two scenarios: steady RPS and burst concurrency.
3) We deliver a report with median/p95 TTFT, chunk cadence latency distribution, and a recommended Dedicated configuration & MAP.

I've attached a small benchmark script (redwood-benchmark-script.sh) and will include placeholder results in benchmark_results_acme.pdf. I'll also drop the MAP draft in the shared Drive (link below).

- Marissa: schedule the short benchmark review (30m)  Tue 7/20 10am PT was proposed; works for me.
